A framework for asking research questions

Start with a simple rule: the two numbers must add up to no more than four. Move the slider to change the limit. The lit pairs show which combinations meet it.

The second view shows a small example from the mathematics of positive responses. Its formula is available if you want it. Neither view tells us which possible state will happen, or whether a real device can reach it.

Move the slider to change the rule. Lit pairs meet the current rule. You can also try a second mathematical view.

Words used here
admissibility
Whether something meets the stated rules or constraints. It does not mean that it will happen or that we can reach it.
positive response
A response described by a number table that gives zero or above for every direction you test. Here, that puts a limit on the shared term c. The formula is available under the calculation details.
Read the fuller explanation

Begin with a small garden of states. Each state carries two quantities. Initially, the declared toy rule permits a total no greater than four. Change the rule and watch the available set change. Then try the positive-response view: the joint relation must also fit the two quantities that support it.

The corpus starts its deeper explanation with admission and composition: which states, observables and responses can coexist positively on a declared carrier? Only after those conditions are specified does it ask how the admitted possibilities transform.

Notice what the garden has not decided. A permitted state is not necessarily reachable from here, stable over time, preferred by anyone, or realized in the world. Keeping those questions apart makes room for a more exact next step.

An overview of the current research

The admissibility frontier

Experiments can erase phase, delay, boundary order, orientation and correlations. The programme asks which distinguishing records an apparatus could preserve. The physical identification of the proposed structures remains open.
